When: we describe a noun. The adjective ending depends on gender, number and definiteness, but there are only three options: no change, -t, -e.
indefinite (en / et / no article) | en stor bil | et stort hus | store biler
after er (… er stor) | Bilen er stor. (The car is big.) | Huset er stort. (The house is big.) | Bilerne er store. (The cars are big.)
definite (den / det / de, min, Peters) | den store bil | det store hus | de store biler

Note: no -t: adjectives ending in -isk and nationalities (dansk, praktisk), in -t (sort, let) and in -e (moderne): et dansk ord (a Danish word), et moderne køkken (a modern kitchen). But frisk → et friskt brød (fresh bread).
Note: lille (small, little) is special: en lille bil, et lille hus, but in the plural it's små: små børn (little children).
Note: an adjective after er also agrees: Vejret er godt. (The weather is nice.) Vi er glade. (We are happy.)
Vi har et stort køkken og to små værelser. — We have a big kitchen and two small rooms.
Huset er gammelt, men haven er smuk. — The house is old, but the garden is beautiful.
When: the result matters now ("I've already done it"), life experience ("I've been there"), or an action that started in the past and is still going on. No specific past time.
Verb | Helper verb (for all persons) | Past participle | Example
-ede group: arbejde, lave | har | arbejdet, lavet | Jeg har arbejdet hele dagen. (I've worked all day.)
-te group: spise, købe | har | spist, købt | Har du spist? (Have you eaten?)
ending in a vowel: bo | har | boet | Vi har boet her i to år. (We've lived here for two years.)
movement somewhere, change of state: gå, komme, blive | er | gået, kommet, blevet | Hun er gået hjem. (She has gone home.)
irregular: være, se, drikke, skrive | har | været, set, drukket, skrevet | Har du set filmen? (Have you seen the movie?)
Note: the helper verb is the same for all persons: jeg har, hun har, de har; jeg er, hun er, de er.
Note: movement with a result — er: Hun er gået hjem. When the process or duration matters — har: Vi har gået i to timer. (We've been walking for two hours.)
Note: with a specific past time (i går, sidste år) — only datid, just like in English: Jeg var i Paris sidste år. (I was in Paris last year.)
Note: an action that is still going on — førnutid, just like English "I have lived": Jeg har boet her i to år. (I've lived here for two years.)
Jeg har aldrig været i Skagen. — I've never been to Skagen.
Toget er kørt. — The train has already left.
Har du spist? — Ja, jeg har lige spist. — Have you eaten? — Yes, I've just eaten.
When: requests, advice, instructions, commands. The same form whether you're talking to one person or several — no endings at all.
Infinitive | How to form it | Imperative | Example
spise, vente, dreje | drop the -e | spis, vent, drej | Vent lidt!
lukke, komme, drikke | drop the -e; the double consonant is simplified | luk, kom, drik | Luk døren!
åbne, cykle | drop the -e, even if that leaves a consonant cluster at the end | åbn, cykl | Åbn vinduet!
gå, se, bo | doesn't end in -e — no change | gå, se, bo | Se her!
være, have | special | vær, hav | Hav en god dag! (Have a nice day!)
Note: just like in English, one form works for one person or many: Luk døren! (Close the door!)
Note: negation: ikke goes after the verb — Glem det ikke! (Don't forget it!) — or Lad være med at + infinitive: Lad være med at råbe! (Don't shout!)
Note: a bare imperative sounds blunt. More polite: Vær sød at lukke døren. (Please close the door.) Kan du lukke døren? (Can you close the door?)
Kom ind og sæt dig! — Come in and sit down!
Drej til højre ved kirken. — Turn right at the church.
When: comparing two things (comparative + end "than") or singling out one from a group (superlative).
most adjectives | billig, varm, ny | billigere, varmere, nyere | billigst, varmest, nyest
vowel change | stor, lang, ung | større, længere, yngre | størst, længst, yngst
irregular | god, gammel, lille, mange | bedre, ældre, mindre, flere | bedst, ældst, mindst, flest
long words | interessant, moderne | mere interessant | mest interessant
Note: "than" is end: Bussen er billigere end toget. (The bus is cheaper than the train.) "As … as" is lige så … som: Hun er lige så høj som sin bror. (She is as tall as her brother.)
Note: after den/det/de, the superlative takes -e: den billigste billet (the cheapest ticket), det bedste sted (the best place).
Note: adjectives ending in -ig take -st, not -est: billigst, hurtigst.
København er større end Aarhus. — Copenhagen is bigger than Aarhus.
Det er den bedste kaffe i byen. — It's the best coffee in town.
